By: James Carroll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Egamers compete for a R1 million pot at the Telkom TGL Masters

Unique Selling Point:
A first for South Africa - competitive video gaming reaches new levels when 8 players go head to head to see who walks away with R1 million. What makes these guys tick and how does competitive e-gaming work?
eSports has until 2016 largely been an underground movement in South Africa. Having said that, PwC benchmarks the South African gaming industry at over R2.6 billion, estimating it will reach R3.6 billion by 2019.
Representatives from the local eSports industry, as well as broadcasters and agencies working in the industry will discuss the size, activities and audience the local gaming community represents and how eSports is likely to become a household viewing activity in South African homes alongside traditional sport and entertainment in years to come.

Summary:
Interviews with the gamers themselves.
https://www.facebook.com/TelkomDGL/photos/a.362329363849775.83433.166360716779975/1100302173385820/?type=3&theater

The voice of esports, Paul 'ReDeYe' Chaloner will be announcing the competition over the weekend. He has been a professional commentator for esports for 15 years.
http://www.espn.co.uk/esports/story/_/id/17416296/paul-redeye-chaloner

Steve Whitford - eSports consultant

Vox pops at the event

Further information:
Filming at Rage expo on Sunday. Claire isn't available but John is in town and would be willing to shoot on Sunday. I would need a commission number as soon as possible so that I can get Ingrid to rebook his flight back down to Cape Town for the evening.

Diego Olliver who shot the Carte Blanche promo is available to shoot.

Press Release:


Online Gaming Explosion
With up to 1.7 billion gamers on the planet, the online games your parents thought were a waste of life could make you rich? Carte Blanche meets South Africa’s top competitive video games, fighting to the virtual death for massive cash prizes and crushing the stereotype of geeks hiding in basements.


Script:


Esports script
14/10/2016

Opening with visuals of game and Bravado winning.

John VO: Professional video gaming or e-sports has grown by leaps and bounds over the last couple of years with the industry generating an estimated $750 million in 2016. South Africa has followed suit where up to 100,000 people are playing online competitively with millions more people spectating live or online. (18s)

John: We’re at Rage in Johannesburg where 600 people are competing in various e-sports for their share of an astonishing R1 million in cash prizes. (10s)

John VO: Over the weekend 8 teams of five players each went head to head at the Telkom Digital Gaming League Masters. (6.5s)

John VO: In the end, two teams were crowned victorious with Bravado Gaming winning the Counter Strike: Global Offensive competition and White Rabbit Gaming winning the DOTA 2 contest. (9s)

John VO: Counter Strike: Global Offensive is a tactical first-person shooter that features updated maps, characters and weapons from classic Counter-Strike games while DOTA 2 is multiplayer online battle arena game of action and strategy, played both professionally and casually by millions of fans worldwide. (18s)

John: What sort of preparation did you have to do for this event?

DIMITRI HADJIPASCHALI: I would say on average, specifically this year, we would have a boot camp, a boot camp is pretty much us getting together in one house for a week. We have that once every two months, once every three months and online from our homes, we practice together about 5-6 hours per day.

ALWYN VENTER: These guys have been practicing incredible hours, they’ve been taking days off, playing through evenings, every single tournament – it’s been really, really hard. The emotion that we’ve felt, the tears that we’ve shed together, it’s all paid off. All credit to these guys, they’ve played amazingly and done so, so well.

John: Thulani Sishi is a former rugby player and now avid gamer. (4s)

John: When people speak about esports, is it really a sport, does it require for example the same kind of dedication, does it give you the same thrill as a game of rugby?

THULANI SISHI: Definitely, I get the same adrenalin rush winning a big game or winning a big match or making a play for your team to win the game. Your team supporting you or picking you up, it’s all relative, the similarities are quite close.
The mental strength you need for a game is the same for gaming – if not more for gaming to be brutally honest.

John: What advice do you have for someone who wants to get into gaming and how to keep a balance like you do?

THULANI SISTI: You need to socialize; you need to eat right and at the end of the day, you neeed to have fun.

JOHN: You all look a little bit exhausted; does it take a lot out of you?

DIMITRI HADJIPASCHALI: It does, it does. We’ve made a lot of commitments this year, a lot of sacrifices by individuals in the team, to win this event, one of the major titles in South Africa as we’ve done and in the next two months we’re heading overseas to China, France to compete in some international events we qualified for so we’re looking forward to that and the practice continues forward from here.

John: Somebody who would know what it takes is Paul “Redeye” Chaloner who is a professional e-sports and video game broadcast host who started his career in 2002 and has seen this digital world transform in the last 15 years. (12s)
** Chaloner – Cha-la-na

John: Tell us about some of the sums involved, especially internationally, I mean it’s actually quite astonishing.

PAUL CHALONER: 11 years ago I play in a tournament where I think we won 200 pounds. Last week I hosted a stage in New York for EL1 and the prize fund for one game was $250,000. The International in August in Seattle - $20.8 million. I just want to emphasize that, not rand, 20.8 million dollars for the championship. The winners got $9.6 million and to give a comparison to real world sports, that’s more per person than what Andy Murray got for winning Wimbledon, it’s more than the German football team got for winning the World Cup and it’s more than any of the players got for winning the NFL Superbowl. We’ve arrived!

John: Besides the vast amounts of money that’s being put forward in the sport, there is also some legitimacy being issued by international authorities. In 2013, Canadian League of Legends player Danny Le became the first pro gamer to receive a United States P-1A visa, a category designated for "Internationally Recognized Athletes" and in 2016 the French government started working on a project to regulate and recognize eSports. (23s)

John: Hard work and dedication is a sentiment that is shared by Alwyn Venter, captain of White Rabbit Gaming. (6s)

ALWYN VENTER: If your kid has got a talent for it, invest in them. It’s no different from any other extra mural activity. I would say any of the time that say Chad Le Clos is putting in or any of the Olympic stars, these guys are putting in between 6 and 14 hours a day. To prepare for something like this, with such a massive prize pool, thanks to Telkom and the DGL, it’s incredible the investment to win that.

John: The prize pool of a million rand was sponsored by Telkom to encourage local teams and give them incentives to play. Jacqui O’Sullivan is excited about the impact they’ve made. (10s)

Jacqui O’Sullivan: It’s really quite amazing – it’s interesting to see how it’s growing every year. The Telkom Digital Gaming League has grown 48% year on year. You can see from here today it’s not just the gaming, it’s the products, it’s the cosplay, it’s a whole culture.

END.
